name: Genesis
oneLine: Beginnings: creation, the human fall, and God's promise to bless the world through Abraham's family.
summary: Genesis opens with God creating everything and calling it good, with human beings made in his image. It then tells how humans turned from God, and how sin spread from one generation to the next. From chapter 12 the focus narrows to one family: Abraham, Isaac, Jacob and Joseph. God makes a covenant (a binding promise) with them, pledging to bless all nations through their descendants. Christians see that promise as the seed of the whole biblical story, finally fulfilled in Jesus.
author: Traditionally Moses; many scholars see several older sources edited over time
date: c. 1440-1400 BC (traditional); many scholars date its final form much later
readingTip: Read chapters 1-3 slowly, then read the Joseph story (chapters 37-50) as one continuous drama.

name: Exodus
oneLine: God rescues Israel from slavery in Egypt, reveals his name, and binds them to himself at Mount Sinai.
summary: Exodus tells how the descendants of Jacob, enslaved in Egypt, cried out and God heard them. He called Moses at the burning bush, revealed his name as “I AM WHO I AM,” and freed his people through plagues and the parting of the sea. At Mount Sinai God gave the Ten Commandments and made a covenant with Israel. The book ends with the tabernacle, a tent where God's presence dwells among them. Christians read the Passover lamb and the rescue from slavery as pictures of salvation through Christ.
author: Traditionally Moses; many scholars see several sources edited over time
readingTip: Read chapters 1-20 as a story, then skim the tabernacle details while asking why God wants to live among his people.

name: Leviticus
oneLine: Laws for worship, sacrifice and holy living, so that a holy God can dwell among an imperfect people.
summary: Leviticus is a handbook for Israel's priests and people. It describes sacrifices, festivals, rules of purity and the Day of Atonement, when the high priest made atonement for the sins of the whole nation. Its central call is “Be holy, because I, the LORD your God, am holy.” It also contains the command Jesus called the second greatest: love your neighbor as yourself. Many first-time readers find it hard going, but Christians read its sacrifices as pointing to the once-for-all sacrifice of Christ, as the Letter to the Hebrews explains.
author: Traditionally Moses; many scholars attribute it to later priestly writers
readingTip: Start with chapter 16 (the Day of Atonement) and chapter 19 (holy living), then read Hebrews 9-10 alongside.

name: Numbers
oneLine: Israel's forty years in the wilderness: grumbling, rebellion, and God's patient faithfulness.
summary: Numbers takes its name from the two censuses (countings) of Israel. Between them lies a sad story. The people rescued from Egypt complain, doubt God's promises and refuse to enter the promised land, so a whole generation wanders in the desert for forty years. Yet God keeps providing manna, water and guidance, and he renews his promise to their children. The book honestly portrays human unbelief alongside God's steady faithfulness. It also holds the priestly blessing that is still spoken in churches today.
author: Traditionally Moses; many scholars see several sources edited over time
readingTip: Read chapters 13-14, the spies' report, to see the turning point of the whole wilderness story.

name: Deuteronomy
oneLine: Moses' farewell sermons: remember what God has done, love him with all your heart, and choose life.
summary: Deuteronomy means “second law.” On the edge of the promised land, the aged Moses retells Israel's story and restates the covenant for a new generation. Its heart is the Shema, Israel's great confession: “The LORD our God, the LORD is One,” followed by the call to love God with all your heart, soul and strength. Moses sets before the people blessing and curse, life and death, and urges them to choose life. When Jesus was tempted in the wilderness, he answered each temptation with words from Deuteronomy.
author: Traditionally Moses (the account of his death added later); many scholars date it to the 7th century BC
readingTip: Read chapters 6-8 and 30, the heart of Moses' appeal, before working through the detailed laws.

name: Joshua
oneLine: Under Joshua, Israel crosses the Jordan and settles the land God promised to Abraham.
summary: Joshua continues the story after Moses' death. God tells Joshua to be strong and courageous, and Israel crosses the Jordan, sees the walls of Jericho fall, and gradually settles Canaan. The land is divided among the tribes, and the book ends with Joshua calling the people to choose whom they will serve. Its accounts of warfare raise hard moral questions that Christians have long wrestled with. Most read them as a unique act of judgment within Israel's history (see Genesis 15:16), never as a pattern for believers today.
author: Traditionally Joshua, with later additions; many scholars date its compilation later
readingTip: Read chapters 1-6 and 23-24; the long land lists in between can be skimmed.

name: Judges
oneLine: A downward spiral: Israel forgets God, falls into trouble, cries out, and is rescued again and again.
summary: After Joshua, Israel has no king. Judges tells of a repeating cycle: the people turn to other gods, fall under oppression, cry out to the LORD, and he raises up a “judge,” a rescuer such as Deborah, Gideon or Samson. But each cycle sinks lower, and the final chapters describe shocking violence. The closing refrain, “everyone did what was right in his own eyes,” shows what happens when people make themselves the measure of right and wrong. Christians see in it both human failure and the long patience of God.
author: Unknown; Jewish tradition names Samuel
readingTip: Read the story of Gideon (chapters 6-8) to see the cycle up close, and be ready for the darkness of the last chapters.

name: Ruth
oneLine: A widow's loyal love and a kinsman's kindness weave a quiet story of providence leading to King David.
summary: Set in the dark days of the judges, Ruth is a short and beautiful story. Naomi, an Israelite widow, loses her husband and sons in a foreign land. Her Moabite daughter-in-law Ruth refuses to leave her, pledging herself to Naomi's people and Naomi's God. In Bethlehem, Ruth meets Boaz, who acts as a “kinsman-redeemer,” a relative who rescues family members in need. Their marriage leads to the birth of King David's grandfather. Without any miracles, the book shows God working through ordinary loyalty and kindness, even toward an outsider.
author: Unknown; Jewish tradition names Samuel
readingTip: Read all four chapters in one sitting; it takes about fifteen minutes.

name: 1 Samuel
oneLine: Israel asks for a king: the stories of Samuel, Saul's tragic reign, and the rise of young David.
summary: First Samuel begins with Hannah's prayer for a child and the birth of Samuel, the last of the judges and a great prophet. The people demand a king “like all the other nations,” and God gives them Saul, tall and impressive but disobedient. God then chooses David, a shepherd boy, because he looks at the heart rather than outward appearance. The book includes David's victory over Goliath, his deep friendship with Saul's son Jonathan, and his years as a fugitive. It asks what real leadership looks like before God.
author: Unknown; tradition names Samuel, with the prophets Nathan and Gad
readingTip: Read chapters 16-18 for David's anointing and Goliath, then chapter 24 to see David spare Saul's life.

name: 2 Samuel
oneLine: David's reign: God's everlasting promise to his house, his grave sin, his repentance, and family sorrow.
summary: Second Samuel tells of David as king. He unites the tribes, makes Jerusalem his capital, and receives a remarkable promise from God through the prophet Nathan: his throne will be established forever. Christians see this promise fulfilled in Jesus, the “Son of David.” But David also commits adultery with Bathsheba and arranges her husband's death. Confronted by Nathan, he repents, yet the consequences ripple through his family in rebellion and grief. The book is unflinchingly honest about the failures of its hero.
author: Unknown; drawing on prophetic records (traditionally Nathan and Gad)
readingTip: Read chapter 7, then chapters 11-12 alongside Psalm 51, David's prayer of repentance.

name: 1 Kings
oneLine: Solomon's wisdom and temple, then a divided kingdom and the prophet Elijah's stand against false gods.
summary: First Kings opens with Solomon, famed for his wisdom, who builds the temple in Jerusalem. At its dedication he prays that the God whom the highest heavens cannot contain will still hear his people. Yet Solomon turns to other gods, and after his death the kingdom splits into Israel in the north and Judah in the south. The second half features Elijah, who confronts King Ahab and the prophets of Baal on Mount Carmel, and later meets God not in wind or fire but in “a still, small voice.”
author: Unknown; Jewish tradition names Jeremiah
readingTip: Read Solomon's prayer in chapter 8, then follow Elijah through chapters 17-19.

name: 2 Kings
oneLine: The kingdoms of Israel and Judah decline, despite the prophets' warnings, until both go into exile.
summary: Second Kings continues the history of the divided kingdom. Elisha succeeds Elijah and performs many acts of mercy. But most kings lead the people into idolatry and injustice. The prophets warn again and again. The northern kingdom falls to Assyria in 722 BC, and Judah, despite the reforms of Hezekiah and Josiah, falls to Babylon in 586 BC. Jerusalem and the temple are destroyed. The book explains the exile as the fruit of covenant unfaithfulness, yet ends with a small sign of hope: David's descendant is still alive.
author: Unknown; Jewish tradition names Jeremiah
readingTip: Read chapters 2-5 for Elisha's stories, then chapter 17 for the book's own explanation of the fall.

name: 1 Chronicles
oneLine: Israel's history retold for returning exiles, centered on David, worship, and God's promises.
summary: Chronicles retells Israel's story for the community that returned from exile in Babylon. First Chronicles begins with long genealogies (family lists) from Adam onward, reminding a small and discouraged people that they belong to a great story. It then focuses on David, especially his preparations for the temple and his organizing of worship and music. It passes lightly over David's failures to emphasize God's promises to his line. Its great prayer of praise declares that everything in heaven and earth belongs to God.
author: Traditionally Ezra; many scholars speak simply of “the Chronicler”
readingTip: Skim the genealogies of chapters 1-9, then read David's prayer in chapter 29.

name: 2 Chronicles
oneLine: From Solomon's temple to the exile and Cyrus's decree, a history told through the lens of worship.
summary: Second Chronicles traces the kings of Judah from Solomon to the Babylonian exile. It pays special attention to the temple and to kings who sought God, such as Jehoshaphat, Hezekiah and Josiah, who led reforms and renewals. A recurring message is that God responds when his people humble themselves, pray and turn back to him. Even wicked King Manasseh is restored when he repents. The book ends not with ruin but with Cyrus of Persia allowing the exiles to go home and rebuild.
author: Traditionally Ezra; many scholars speak simply of “the Chronicler”
readingTip: Read chapters 6-7, then chapter 33, where Manasseh's repentance shows how far God's mercy reaches.

name: Ezra
oneLine: Exiles return from Babylon to rebuild the temple and re-center their life on God's word.
summary: Ezra tells of the return of Jewish exiles from Babylon after the Persian king Cyrus allowed them to go home in 538 BC. The first group rebuilds the temple despite opposition. Decades later Ezra, a priest and scribe, arrives having set his heart to study, practice and teach the Law of God. He leads the people in confession and renewal. For Christians the book shows God keeping his promises even through the decisions of foreign kings, and a people rebuilt around Scripture.
author: Traditionally Ezra
readingTip: Read chapters 1, 3 and 7 to see the return, the rebuilding and Ezra's mission.

name: Nehemiah
oneLine: Nehemiah rebuilds Jerusalem's walls through prayer and hard work, and the people renew their covenant.
summary: Nehemiah, a Jewish official serving the Persian king, hears that Jerusalem's walls lie in ruins. He prays, asks the king for leave, and organizes the people to rebuild in just fifty-two days, despite mockery and threats. Much of the book is his own first-person memoir. When the work is done, Ezra reads the Law aloud, the people weep, and they are told that the joy of the LORD is their strength. Nehemiah combines practical leadership with constant, brief prayers.
author: Nehemiah (memoirs), perhaps compiled with Ezra
readingTip: Notice the short prayers Nehemiah breathes in the middle of action, as in 2:4 and 4:9.

name: Esther
oneLine: A Jewish queen in Persia risks her life to save her people, in a book where God is never named.
summary: Esther, a young Jewish woman, becomes queen of Persia. When the official Haman plots to destroy all the Jews in the empire, her cousin Mordecai urges her to speak to the king, suggesting she may have come to her position “for such a time as this.” At great risk she intercedes, and the plot is turned back on Haman. God is never mentioned in the book, yet Jews and Christians alike see his hidden hand in its remarkable reversals. It is the origin of the Jewish festival of Purim.
author: Unknown
readingTip: Read it in one sitting like a short novel, and watch for the reversals of fortune.

name: Job
oneLine: A righteous man loses everything and wrestles with God over why the innocent suffer.
summary: Job is a blameless man who loses his wealth, his children and his health. In long poetic speeches, three friends insist he must have sinned, since suffering is punishment; Job protests his innocence and demands an answer from God. At last God speaks from a whirlwind, not explaining the reason but revealing the vastness and wisdom of creation. Job is humbled and comforted, and God says Job spoke rightly, unlike his friends. The book refuses easy answers to suffering, yet insists that God is present and sovereign.
author: Unknown
date: Uncertain; set in the age of the patriarchs, written perhaps in Solomon's era or later
readingTip: Read chapters 1-3, then jump to God's speeches in chapters 38-42, and return to the dialogues later.

name: Psalms
oneLine: Israel's songbook and prayer book: 150 poems of praise, lament, trust, confession and longing.
summary: The Psalms are 150 songs and prayers gathered over many centuries. They cover the whole range of human feeling: joy, fear, anger, grief, guilt, gratitude and wonder. Some praise God as creator and king; others cry “How long, O LORD?” from the depths. Christians have prayed the Psalms daily for two thousand years, and Jesus himself prayed them, even on the cross. Calvin called the book an anatomy of every part of the soul, because every human emotion finds its reflection there.
author: David (73 psalms bear his name), with Asaph, the sons of Korah, Solomon, Moses and others
readingTip: Start with Psalms 1, 8, 23, 51, 103 and 139, and try reading one aloud as a prayer.

name: Proverbs
oneLine: Short, memorable sayings on wisdom for everyday life: words, work, money, friendship and family.
summary: Proverbs is a collection of wise sayings, many attributed to King Solomon. Its opening chapters are a father's appeal to his son to seek wisdom, pictured as a woman calling out in the streets. The rest is mostly short, punchy observations about speech, honesty, hard work, money, anger, friendship and family. Its foundation is that “the fear of the LORD,” a reverent awe before God, is the beginning of knowledge. Proverbs describes how life generally works: they are wise patterns, not guaranteed promises.
author: Mainly Solomon, with Agur, Lemuel and other wise teachers
date: c. 950-700 BC (collected under Solomon and later Hezekiah)
readingTip: Read one chapter a day for a month, matching the chapter to the date.

name: Ecclesiastes
oneLine: A searching meditation on the meaning of life under the sun, where everything seems a passing breath.
summary: Ecclesiastes is the reflection of “the Teacher,” who tests every path to meaning: pleasure, work, wealth, wisdom and achievement. His refrain, “futility of futilities” (older translations say “vanity of vanities”), uses the Hebrew word hevel, meaning vapor or breath: life is fleeting and hard to grasp. Death comes to wise and foolish alike. Yet he commends enjoying food, work and love as gifts from God, and observes that God has set eternity in the human heart. His conclusion: fear God and keep his commandments.
author: Traditionally Solomon; many scholars date it after the exile
readingTip: Treat it as an honest conversation partner for your own questions about meaning, and read it to the end.

name: Song of Songs
oneLine: Love poems celebrating the delight and faithfulness of love between a bride and her beloved.
summary: The Song of Songs, also called the Song of Solomon, is a series of poems in which a bride and groom speak of their longing for and delight in each other. It celebrates romantic and physical love within committed faithfulness as a good gift of God. For centuries Jewish and Christian readers have also read it as a picture of God's love for his people, and of Christ's love for the church. Many Protestant interpreters today hold both readings together: human love honored for its own sake, and pointing beyond itself.
author: Traditionally Solomon; authorship is debated
readingTip: Read it as poetry, enjoying the imagery, then reread chapter 8 slowly.

name: Isaiah
oneLine: The great prophet of God's holiness, judgment and comfort, foreseeing a coming servant and king.
summary: Isaiah prophesied in Jerusalem in the eighth century BC. He saw the Lord “high and exalted” and was sent to warn Judah against injustice and idolatry. His book moves from judgment to comfort: chapters 40-66 speak to exiles of a God who will bring them home and make all things new. It holds the Old Testament's clearest portraits of the Messiah, including a child called “Mighty God” and a suffering servant “pierced for our transgressions.” The New Testament quotes Isaiah more than any other prophet.
author: Isaiah son of Amoz; many scholars assign chapters 40-66 to later disciples
readingTip: Read chapters 6, 9, 40 and 52:13-53:12 first; these are its mountain peaks.

name: Jeremiah
oneLine: The weeping prophet warns Jerusalem of judgment and promises a new covenant written on the heart.
summary: Jeremiah was called as a young man and prophesied for about forty years as Judah slid toward destruction by Babylon. His message of coming judgment made him hated: he was beaten, imprisoned and lowered into a muddy cistern. He is often called “the weeping prophet,” and his book includes raw prayers of complaint to God. Yet it also holds one of Scripture's great promises: a new covenant in which God will write his law on human hearts and forgive sins. Christians believe Jesus inaugurated this covenant.
author: Jeremiah, with his scribe Baruch
readingTip: Read chapter 1 for his calling, then chapters 31-32, where hope shines in the darkest hour.

name: Lamentations
oneLine: Five poems of grief over Jerusalem's destruction, with a surprising confession of hope at the center.
summary: Lamentations mourns the fall of Jerusalem to Babylon in 586 BC. Its five poems describe famine, ruin and shame without softening anything. Four of them are acrostics, each verse or stanza beginning with the next letter of the Hebrew alphabet, as though giving grief an orderly shape from A to Z. At the very center, the poet remembers that the LORD's mercies are new every morning. The book shows that lament, bringing pain honestly before God, is itself an act of faith.
author: Traditionally Jeremiah; the book itself is anonymous
readingTip: Read chapter 3 slowly and notice the exact point where despair turns toward hope.

name: Ezekiel
oneLine: A priest in exile sees God's glory leave the temple, then foresees new hearts and dry bones made alive.
summary: Ezekiel was a priest taken to Babylon with the exiles. His book opens with a dazzling vision of God's glory, showing that God is not confined to Jerusalem. Through strange symbolic actions and visions, he announces that the temple will fall because of the people's sins, and he sees God's glory depart from it. After the fall, his message turns to hope: God will give his people a new heart and a new spirit, and in a valley of dry bones he sees a dead nation breathe again.
author: Ezekiel
readingTip: Read chapter 1 for the vision, then 36:22-37:14 for the promise of new life.

name: Daniel
oneLine: Faithful exiles in Babylon, and visions of world empires giving way to God's everlasting kingdom.
summary: Daniel has two halves. Chapters 1-6 are stories of Daniel and his friends, young Jewish exiles who stay faithful in the court of Babylon, surviving a fiery furnace and a den of lions. Chapters 7-12 are apocalyptic visions, a kind of symbolic prophecy that unveils God's hidden purposes in history. In them, beastly empires rise and fall until God gives an everlasting kingdom to “One like the Son of Man.” Jesus made “Son of Man” his favorite way of speaking about himself.
author: Traditionally Daniel; many scholars date the visions to c. 165 BC
readingTip: Read the stories in chapters 1-6 first, then chapter 7 alongside Mark 14:61-62.

name: Hosea
oneLine: A prophet's heartbreaking marriage becomes a picture of God's faithful love for unfaithful Israel.
summary: God tells Hosea to marry Gomer, who proves unfaithful. Hosea's painful marriage becomes a living parable of Israel's unfaithfulness to God through idolatry, and of God's refusal to give up on them. The book is full of tender and fierce images: God as a betrayed husband, and as a parent who taught a child to walk. Judgment is real, but love has the last word. Jesus twice quoted Hosea's line that God desires mercy, not sacrifice.
author: Hosea
readingTip: Read chapters 1-3 for the story, then chapter 11 for the heart of God.

name: Joel
oneLine: A locust plague becomes a call to return to God, with the promise of the Spirit poured on all people.
summary: Joel describes a devastating locust plague and treats it as a warning of “the Day of the LORD,” a coming time of judgment. He calls the people to fast, to rend their hearts and not their garments, and to return to a God who is gracious and compassionate. Then comes promise: God will repay the years the locusts have eaten and pour out his Spirit on all people, young and old, men and women. At Pentecost, Peter declared that this prophecy was being fulfilled.
author: Joel son of Pethuel
date: Uncertain; proposals range from the 9th to the 4th century BC
readingTip: Read chapter 2, then Acts 2 to see how Peter applied it.

name: Amos
oneLine: A shepherd from Judah confronts the wealthy north: worship without justice is worthless to God.
summary: Amos was a shepherd and tender of fig trees, not a professional prophet, sent to the prosperous northern kingdom of Israel. He condemned the wealthy for trampling the poor, taking bribes and selling the needy for a pair of sandals, all while keeping up lavish religious festivals. God, he says, hates such worship. He wants justice to roll on like a river instead. The book ends with a promise that God will restore the fallen house of David.
author: Amos of Tekoa
readingTip: Read chapters 1-2 to feel the surprise ending of his opening speech, then read chapter 5.

name: Obadiah
oneLine: The shortest Old Testament book: judgment on proud Edom for betraying its brother nation, Judah.
summary: Obadiah is a single chapter of twenty-one verses aimed at Edom, a neighboring nation descended from Jacob's brother Esau. When Jerusalem fell, Edom gloated, looted and handed over refugees. Obadiah announces that Edom's pride has deceived it, and that as it has done, so it will be done to it. The book ends with a vision of the kingdom belonging to the LORD. It raises lasting questions about pride, cruelty toward a neighbor in trouble, and the justice of God.
author: Obadiah
readingTip: Read it with Genesis 27 and Psalm 137 to see the long story of Jacob and Esau's descendants.

name: Jonah
oneLine: A reluctant prophet runs from God, is swallowed by a great fish, and resents God's mercy to his enemies.
summary: God sends Jonah to Nineveh, the capital of Assyria, Israel's brutal enemy. Jonah flees by ship, is thrown overboard, and is swallowed by a great fish, where he prays. Given a second chance, he preaches, and the whole city repents. God spares them, and Jonah is furious, because he knew God was gracious and compassionate. The book ends with God asking a question about caring for a great city. Jesus pointed to Jonah's three days in the fish as a sign of his own death and resurrection.
author: Traditionally Jonah or an associate; many scholars date it later and read it as a teaching story
readingTip: Read all four chapters at once, and notice that the book ends with a question left open for you.

name: Micah
oneLine: A prophet of justice who names what God requires and foretells a ruler born in Bethlehem.
summary: Micah, a contemporary of Isaiah from a small country town, spoke against corrupt leaders, greedy landowners and false prophets in both Israel and Judah. He warned that Jerusalem would become a heap of rubble. Yet he also foresaw a ruler coming from little Bethlehem, a passage the Gospels connect with Jesus' birth. His most famous line sums up the heart of true religion: to act justly, to love mercy, and to walk humbly with God. The book closes in wonder at a God who pardons sin.
author: Micah of Moresheth
readingTip: Read chapters 5-7, ending with 7:18-20 on the God who delights in mercy.

name: Nahum
oneLine: A poem announcing Nineveh's fall: God is slow to anger but will not leave cruelty unpunished.
summary: About a century after Jonah, Assyria had returned to its cruelty, conquering Israel and terrorizing the region. Nahum's vivid poetry announces the fall of its capital, Nineveh, which came in 612 BC. The book opens with a hymn to God's power, declaring that the LORD is slow to anger but will by no means leave the guilty unpunished. For people who had suffered under a brutal empire, this was comfort: the LORD is good, a stronghold in the day of distress, and evil will not have the last word.
author: Nahum of Elkosh
readingTip: Read it after Jonah, and ask how God's mercy and God's justice belong together.

name: Habakkuk
oneLine: A prophet questions God about injustice and learns that the righteous will live by faith.
summary: Habakkuk is a dialogue between a prophet and God. Habakkuk complains that violence goes unpunished in Judah. God replies that he is raising up the Babylonians to judge them, which only deepens the question: how can a holy God use a more wicked nation? God answers that the proud will fall, but the righteous will live by faith. Paul quotes this line in Romans and Galatians, and it later helped spark Luther's Reformation. The book ends with a song of trust even when the fig tree does not bud.
author: Habakkuk
readingTip: Read all three chapters and notice how the honest questions of chapter 1 lead to the song of chapter 3.

name: Zephaniah
oneLine: Warnings of the coming Day of the LORD, ending in a song of a God who rejoices over his people.
summary: Zephaniah prophesied in the days of King Josiah, probably before his great reforms. He warns of the coming Day of the LORD against Judah and the nations, a day of darkness for the proud and complacent who think God will do nothing. He calls the humble to seek the LORD. The book ends with one of the most tender passages in the prophets: God in the midst of his people, mighty to save, quieting them with his love and rejoicing over them with singing.
author: Zephaniah, a descendant of King Hezekiah
readingTip: Read chapter 3 first, then return to chapter 1 to feel the contrast.

name: Haggai
oneLine: A call to returned exiles to stop neglecting God's house and rebuild the temple.
summary: Haggai delivered four short messages in 520 BC to Jews who had returned from exile. They had begun rebuilding the temple, then stopped and turned to their own houses and fields, yet nothing seemed to prosper. Haggai tells them to consider their ways and get to work. The people respond, and God promises to be with them and to fill the new house with a glory greater than the former. Christians see that promise fulfilled when Jesus taught in this rebuilt temple.
author: Haggai
readingTip: Read both chapters in one sitting, noting the exact dates that frame each message.

name: Zechariah
oneLine: Night visions and promises for a rebuilding people, including a humble king riding on a donkey.
summary: Zechariah, a contemporary of Haggai, encouraged the returned exiles with eight night visions full of horses, lampstands and scrolls. God's work would succeed “not by might nor by power, but by My Spirit.” The later chapters look further ahead: to a coming king, righteous and humble, riding on a donkey; to a shepherd who is struck down; and to a day when the LORD will be king over all the earth. The Gospels draw on Zechariah repeatedly in describing the last week of Jesus' life.
author: Zechariah; some scholars assign chapters 9-14 to a later prophet
readingTip: Read 9:9-10, then Matthew 21:1-11 to see the prophecy enacted.

name: Malachi
oneLine: The last Old Testament prophet challenges tired worship and promises a messenger to prepare God's way.
summary: Malachi, whose name means “my messenger,” speaks to a community that has grown weary and cynical about God. The book is a series of disputes: God makes a claim, the people object, and God answers. He confronts careless offerings, broken marriages and injustice. Yet it begins with “I have loved you,” and it ends with the promise of a messenger, like Elijah, who will prepare the way before the Lord comes. The New Testament identifies this messenger with John the Baptist.
author: Malachi
readingTip: Read it last in the Old Testament, then turn straight to Mark 1:1-8.

name: Matthew
oneLine: Jesus as the promised Messiah and King who fulfills the Scriptures and teaches the way of his kingdom.
summary: Matthew was written with Jewish readers in mind. It begins with Jesus' family line from Abraham and David and repeatedly shows how his life fulfills the Old Testament. Jesus is “Immanuel,” God with us. Matthew gathers Jesus' teaching into five great speeches, including the Sermon on the Mount, and presents him as the King whose kingdom of heaven turns the world's values upside down. The book ends with the risen Jesus sending his followers to make disciples of all nations, promising to be with them always.
author: Traditionally Matthew (Levi), the tax collector and apostle; the Gospel itself is anonymous
readingTip: Read the Sermon on the Mount (chapters 5-7) early, then the last three chapters.

name: Mark
oneLine: The shortest, fastest Gospel: Jesus' deeds, the question “Who do you say I am?”, and the cross.
summary: Mark is the shortest Gospel and probably the earliest. It moves quickly, often using the word “immediately.” Jesus heals, casts out demons, calms storms and forgives sins, while people keep asking, “Who is this?” At the midpoint Peter confesses that Jesus is the Christ. From then on Jesus heads toward Jerusalem and the cross, teaching that the Son of Man came to serve and to give his life as a ransom for many. Early church tradition says Mark recorded the preaching of Peter.
author: John Mark, drawing on Peter's preaching (early church tradition)
readingTip: Read it in one or two sittings, as it was probably meant to be heard aloud from start to finish.

name: Luke
oneLine: A careful account of Jesus' life, with special care for the poor, outsiders, women and the lost.
summary: Luke, a physician and companion of Paul, investigated eyewitness accounts to write an orderly account for a man named Theophilus. His Gospel includes the fullest story of Jesus' birth and many parables found nowhere else, such as the Good Samaritan and the Prodigal Son. Luke shows Jesus' compassion for the poor, the sick, women, Samaritans and notorious sinners, and how often he withdrew to pray. Its theme is summed up in one line: the Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost.
author: Luke the physician, companion of Paul
readingTip: Read chapter 15, Jesus' three stories of lost things, as a window into the whole Gospel.

name: John
oneLine: The reflective Gospel: Jesus as the eternal Word made flesh, who gives life to all who believe.
summary: John begins before time: “In the beginning was the Word,” the Word who was with God and was God, and who became flesh in Jesus. Built around signs (miracles that point beyond themselves) and “I am” sayings, such as “I am the bread of life” and “I am the resurrection and the life,” it invites readers to see who Jesus is. It also records long, searching conversations with Nicodemus, a Samaritan woman, and the disciples on the night before he died. John states his purpose plainly: that you may believe and have life.
author: John the apostle, “the disciple whom Jesus loved” (traditional)
readingTip: Start with the prologue (1:1-18), then read a chapter a day and ask what each sign reveals.

name: Acts
oneLine: The Holy Spirit comes, and the good news of Jesus spreads from Jerusalem to Rome.
summary: Acts is the second volume of Luke's work. It begins with the risen Jesus ascending and promising the Holy Spirit. At Pentecost the Spirit comes, Peter preaches, and the church is born. The story follows the message as it spreads outward, through persecution and surprise, to Samaritans and non-Jews. Saul, a persecutor, meets the risen Christ and becomes Paul, the great missionary. The book ends with Paul in Rome, under house arrest yet still proclaiming the kingdom of God boldly.
author: Luke, companion of Paul
readingTip: Read chapters 1-2 and 9, then Paul's speech to the philosophers of Athens in chapter 17.

name: Romans
oneLine: Paul's fullest account of the gospel: all have sinned, and God freely justifies those who believe.
summary: Romans is Paul's most systematic letter, written to a church he had not yet visited. He argues that all people, Jews and Gentiles alike, have fallen short of God's glory, and that God's righteousness is given as a gift through faith in Jesus, whose death made atonement for sin. He then explores new life in the Spirit, the place of Israel in God's plan, and how believers should live together in love. Luther's rediscovery of its message helped spark the Reformation, and no letter has shaped Protestant faith more.
author: Paul
readingTip: Read chapters 1-8 as one argument, pausing at 3:21-26, then read chapter 12 to see how it is lived.

name: 1 Corinthians
oneLine: Paul writes to a gifted but divided church about the wisdom of the cross, love, and the resurrection.
summary: Corinth was a wealthy, cosmopolitan port city, and its young church was full of gifts and problems: rival factions, sexual immorality, lawsuits, disorder in worship, and confusion about the resurrection. Paul answers each issue by pointing back to Christ crucified, whose cross looks like foolishness to the world but is the wisdom of God. The letter includes the famous chapter on love (13) and the earliest written summary of the gospel, with the claim that the risen Jesus appeared to more than five hundred people (15).
author: Paul
readingTip: Read chapters 1, 13 and 15 first, then the rest to see love applied to real problems.

name: 2 Corinthians
oneLine: Paul's most personal letter: strength in weakness, comfort in suffering, and new creation in Christ.
summary: Second Corinthians is Paul's most personal letter. Some in Corinth questioned his authority and preferred impressive “super-apostles.” Paul responds not by boasting of strength but by speaking of his hardships, his anxieties and a painful “thorn in my flesh.” God told him that his grace is sufficient, for his power is perfected in weakness. The letter also holds rich teaching on comfort in suffering, on the believer as a new creation, and on God reconciling the world to himself in Christ.
author: Paul
readingTip: Read chapters 4-5 on treasure in jars of clay, then chapter 12.

name: Galatians
oneLine: A passionate defense of the gospel: we are justified by faith in Christ, not by works of the law.
summary: Paul writes urgently to churches in Galatia, in modern Turkey, where teachers insisted that non-Jewish believers must be circumcised and keep the law of Moses to be fully accepted by God. Paul calls this “a different gospel.” A person is justified, declared right with God, by faith in Christ and not by works of the law. Christ has set believers free, not to indulge themselves but to serve one another in love as the Spirit produces his fruit. Luther prized this letter above almost all others.
author: Paul
readingTip: Read it in one sitting, then reread 2:15-21 and 5:13-26 slowly.

name: Ephesians
oneLine: God's grand plan to unite all things in Christ, and a new humanity formed by grace.
summary: Ephesians opens with a soaring hymn of praise for every blessing God has given in Christ, who chose his people before the creation of the world. It declares that we are saved by grace through faith, not by works, and that Christ has broken down the wall between Jews and Gentiles to create one new humanity. The second half shows what this means in daily life: unity, truthful speech, forgiveness, marriage, family and work. It ends with the call to put on the full armor of God.
author: Paul (some scholars think a later disciple wrote in his name)
readingTip: Read 2:1-10 first; it holds the heart of the letter in ten verses.

name: Philippians
oneLine: A letter of joy written from prison, centered on Christ who humbled himself as a servant.
summary: Paul wrote Philippians in chains, perhaps in Rome, to a church that had supported him generously. It is warm and full of joy despite his circumstances. At its center is a hymn about Christ, who existed in the form of God yet emptied himself, took the form of a servant and died on a cross, and whom God has highly exalted. Paul urges his readers to share this humble mind, to rejoice in the Lord always, and to know the peace of God that surpasses all understanding.
author: Paul
readingTip: Read it in one sitting and notice how often joy and rejoicing appear.

name: Colossians
oneLine: Christ supreme over all creation, in whom all things hold together, and the full life found in him.
summary: Paul writes to a church in Colossae troubled by teachers who offered special spiritual knowledge, rituals and visions as a path to fullness. Paul answers with a magnificent portrait of Christ: the image of the invisible God, through whom and for whom all things were created, and in whom all things hold together. Because all the fullness of God dwells in Christ, believers need nothing added. The letter then turns to new life: setting the mind on things above, and putting on compassion, forgiveness and love.
author: Paul (some scholars question this)
readingTip: Read 1:15-20 slowly, asking what it would mean for all things to hold together in a person.

name: 1 Thessalonians
oneLine: Encouragement to a young church facing persecution, with hope for believers who have died.
summary: First Thessalonians is probably Paul's earliest surviving letter. He had to leave Thessalonica in a hurry after a short stay, and he writes with deep affection to new believers who are standing firm under persecution. Some of them were grieving loved ones who had died, and wondered whether they had missed Christ's return. Paul assures them that because Jesus died and rose again, those who have died in him will rise too, so they need not grieve like those who have no hope.
author: Paul, with Silas and Timothy
readingTip: Read 4:13-5:11 and notice how Paul uses future hope to shape present life.

name: 2 Thessalonians
oneLine: Correcting confusion about the Day of the Lord, and urging believers to keep working and doing good.
summary: Soon after his first letter, Paul writes again to Thessalonica. Some believers had been unsettled by claims that the Day of the Lord had already come, and some had stopped working, perhaps expecting the end at any moment. Paul explains that certain events must happen first, encourages the church in its sufferings with the promise of God's justice, and tells the idle to earn their own living. He urges everyone not to grow weary in doing good.
author: Paul (some scholars question this)
readingTip: Read it right after 1 Thessalonians, as the second half of one conversation.

name: 1 Timothy
oneLine: Paul's guidance to his young colleague Timothy on leading a church in truth and godliness.
summary: First Timothy is one of the “Pastoral Letters,” written to guide church leaders. Paul writes to Timothy, whom he left in Ephesus to counter false teaching. He gives instructions for prayer and worship, describes the qualities needed in overseers (elders) and deacons, and warns against the love of money. Along the way he offers some of the clearest summaries of the faith: that Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners, and that there is one mediator between God and humanity, the man Christ Jesus.
author: Paul; many scholars think a later follower wrote the Pastoral Letters
readingTip: Read 1:12-17, Paul's own story of mercy, then chapter 6 on contentment.

name: 2 Timothy
oneLine: Paul's last letter from prison: guard the gospel, endure hardship, and hold fast to Scripture.
summary: Second Timothy is probably Paul's final letter, written from a Roman prison as he expected execution. Many friends have deserted him, and he asks Timothy to come quickly, bringing his cloak and his scrolls. He urges Timothy not to be ashamed of the gospel, to endure hardship like a good soldier, and to remain in the Scriptures, which are God-breathed and make one wise for salvation. He ends with calm confidence: he has fought the good fight, finished the race and kept the faith.
author: Paul; many scholars think a later follower wrote the Pastoral Letters
readingTip: Read chapter 4 to hear an old man's last words to a younger friend.

name: Titus
oneLine: Instructions for churches on Crete, grounded in the grace of God that saves and transforms.
summary: Paul writes to Titus, his co-worker, whom he left on the island of Crete to appoint elders in every town. He describes the character needed in leaders and calls believers of every age and station to live self-controlled, upright and godly lives. Twice he grounds this teaching in compact summaries of the gospel: God saved us not by righteous deeds we had done but according to his mercy, through renewal by the Holy Spirit. Grace, Paul says, both saves us and trains us to live well.
author: Paul; many scholars think a later follower wrote the Pastoral Letters
readingTip: Read 2:11-14 and 3:3-7, the two gospel summaries at the letter's heart.

name: Philemon
oneLine: A personal appeal to receive a runaway slave back as a beloved brother in Christ.
summary: Philemon is a short personal letter. Onesimus, a slave who had apparently wronged his master Philemon and run away, met Paul and became a Christian. Paul sends him back with this letter, urging Philemon to welcome him “no longer as a slave, but better than a slave, as a beloved brother,” and offering to repay any debt himself. Paul does not directly condemn slavery as an institution, and the letter was later cited on both sides of the slavery debate, but its vision of brotherhood in Christ cuts deeply against it.
author: Paul
readingTip: Read it in five minutes, and notice how Paul persuades with love rather than command.

name: Hebrews
oneLine: Jesus is greater than angels, Moses and the priests: hold fast to him and do not drift away.
summary: Hebrews is a sermon in letter form, written to Christians, probably of Jewish background, who were tempted to drift back under pressure. Its argument is that Jesus is greater than all that came before: the prophets, the angels, Moses and the priesthood. He is the eternal Son and our great high priest, able to sympathize with our weaknesses, who offered himself once for all as the perfect sacrifice. Its famous chapter 11 celebrates the faith of the Old Testament saints.
author: Unknown; once attributed to Paul, with Barnabas and Apollos also suggested
readingTip: Read chapters 1, 4:14-5:10 and 11-12, keeping Leviticus 16 in mind.

name: James
oneLine: Practical wisdom for real faith: endure trials, tame the tongue, care for the poor, and do the word.
summary: James reads like Old Testament wisdom and echoes the Sermon on the Mount. In short, direct sections he tells believers to ask God for wisdom, to endure trials, to control their speech, to show no favoritism to the rich, and to care for orphans and widows. His claim that faith without works is dead once troubled Luther, who called it a letter “of straw” compared with Paul. Most Protestants see no contradiction: we are saved by faith alone, but saving faith is never alone.
author: James, brother of Jesus and leader of the Jerusalem church (traditional)
date: c. AD 45-50, perhaps the earliest New Testament book
readingTip: Read one chapter a day for five days, and choose one command to practice each day.

name: 1 Peter
oneLine: Hope for suffering believers living as foreigners in the world and following Christ's example.
summary: Peter writes to scattered believers in Asia Minor, now Turkey, who face hostility and slander for their faith. He reminds them that through the resurrection of Jesus they have been born again to a living hope and an inheritance that can never perish. As “foreigners and exiles,” they are to live honorably, to answer insults with blessing, and to follow the example of Christ, who suffered without retaliating. They should always be ready to give the reason for their hope, with gentleness and respect.
author: Peter the apostle, with Silvanus' help; some scholars doubt this
readingTip: Read chapter 1 for the living hope, then 2:18-25 and 3:13-18 on suffering well.

name: 2 Peter
oneLine: A farewell warning against false teachers, and the promise of a new heaven and a new earth.
summary: Second Peter presents itself as the apostle's final testament, written as he faced death. It urges believers to grow in virtue, and reminds them that the apostles did not follow clever fables but were eyewitnesses of Christ's majesty. Scripture, it says, came not from human will, but as people were carried along by the Holy Spirit. It warns against teachers who mock the promise of Christ's return, explaining that God's apparent delay is patience, giving time for repentance, until he brings a new heaven and a new earth.
author: Peter the apostle (traditional); widely questioned by modern scholars
readingTip: Read 1:16-21 on eyewitnesses and Scripture, then chapter 3 on patience and hope.

name: 1 John
oneLine: God is light and God is love: marks of true faith and the assurance of eternal life.
summary: First John was written to reassure believers after a group had left their church, denying that Jesus had truly come in the flesh. The letter circles around a few great themes: God is light, so walk in the truth; God is love, so love one another; and Jesus truly came in the flesh. It defines love not by our love for God but by his sending his Son as an atoning sacrifice for our sins. Its purpose is assurance: that you may know you have eternal life.
author: John the apostle (traditional)
readingTip: Read 1:1-2:2 and 4:7-21, the letter's twin peaks.

name: 2 John
oneLine: A brief note urging a church to walk in truth and love and to beware of deceivers.
summary: Second John is a short letter from “the elder” to “the chosen lady and her children,” probably a church and its members. It rejoices that some are walking in the truth, repeats the command to love one another, and defines love as walking according to God's commandments. It also warns against deceivers who deny that Jesus Christ came in the flesh, and tells the church not to give such teachers a platform. Truth and love, it insists, belong together.
author: “The elder,” traditionally John the apostle
readingTip: Read it alongside 1 John, noticing how the same themes are compressed into a few lines.

name: 3 John
oneLine: A personal letter praising generous hospitality and rebuking a church leader who loves to be first.
summary: Third John is one of the shortest books in the Bible. The elder writes to his friend Gaius, praising him for welcoming traveling teachers of the gospel even though they were strangers. He contrasts this with Diotrephes, a local leader who loves to be first, refuses to welcome others and spreads malicious talk. A third man, Demetrius, is well spoken of by everyone. The letter is a small window into the real life of the early churches, with both their generosity and their power struggles.
author: “The elder,” traditionally John the apostle
readingTip: Read it in two minutes and ask which of its three people you most resemble.

name: Jude
oneLine: A short, urgent call to contend for the faith, ending in one of Scripture's great doxologies.
summary: Jude, a brother of James and of Jesus, had meant to write about the salvation believers share. Instead he urges them to contend for the faith, because ungodly people have slipped in, turning God's grace into an excuse for immorality. Using vivid examples from the Old Testament and Jewish tradition, including words from the book of 1 Enoch, he warns of judgment. Yet he tells believers to keep themselves in God's love and to have mercy on those who doubt. It ends with a magnificent doxology, a hymn of praise.
author: Jude, brother of James and of Jesus
readingTip: Read verses 20-25 aloud; the closing words are often spoken as a blessing at the end of services.

name: Revelation
oneLine: Visions of the risen Christ, the struggle between good and evil, and the renewal of all things.
summary: Revelation records visions given to John while exiled on the island of Patmos. It begins with messages from the risen Christ to seven churches, then unfolds in dramatic symbols: a throne room in heaven, a slain Lamb who alone is worthy, seals, trumpets, beasts and the fall of Babylon. Christians interpret its details in different ways, but its central message is clear: Christ has conquered, evil will be judged, and God will dwell with his people in a new heaven and new earth, where he wipes away every tear.
author: John, traditionally the apostle; some think another John
readingTip: Read chapters 1, 4-5 and 21-22 first, and look for the big picture rather than decoding every symbol.
